content: "Instead of consigning your winter garden cuttings to the bonfire or the shredder, consider transforming them into a dead hedge. Built from your prunings, this informal barrier makes an excellent windbreak, provides shelter for wildlife and can neatly delineate different parts of your plot. Drive stakes or reclaimed fence posts into the ground in two parallel rows about 50cm apart, then weave or pile the cut material between them, starting with the thicker branches at the bottom; expect the structure to compact and sink a little as it seasons. If you missed out on any good presents over the holidays, brighten your year by ordering The Book Of Seeds (Ivy Press, £30) by Paul Smith, formerly in charge of Kew’s Millennium Seed Bank. Due for publication in February, it’s an opulent compendium of 600 of the planet’s most unusual and attractive seed types, ranging from a black seed with an amusingly coiffed tuft to orchid seeds barely the size of a pinhead. For winter interest in the garden, try winter-flowering clematis: when given a sunny, sheltered site they can produce blooms from December through February. Varieties such as Clematis cirrhosa ‘Advent Bells’, C. cirrhosa var. balearica and C. cirrhosa ‘Jingle Bells’ offer creamy, scented or pure white flowers and grow to different sizes depending on the selection. Is there anything else I can help with?."
